## What's new in SBK 10.7

SBK 10.7 is a measurement-integrity and object-storage benchmarking release.
It makes successful benchmark output substantially more trustworthy under
asynchronous completion and saturated shutdown, gives Dell ECS, ObjectScale,
MinIO, and other S3-compatible systems a deeper workload-control surface, and
keeps the successful record path focused on low latency and high throughput.

### Highlight: results you can trust at the end of a run

Timed, asynchronous, and distributed benchmarks now preserve a stronger
end-to-end result contract.

- SBK quiesces writers and readers before PerL receives its terminal marker,
  allowing already accepted asynchronous completions to reach the recorder.
- PerL drains producer-quiesced queue shards before publishing `Total`; a
  terminal marker no longer causes queued measurements to be silently dropped.
- Timed `Total` duration remains the requested benchmark duration. Cleanup and
  terminal-marker processing no longer dilute reported throughput.
- A run cannot exit successfully without a clean final PerL completion. If the
  bounded cleanup deadline expires before final results are available, SBK
  exits nonzero rather than reporting an empty successful benchmark.
- Queue ownership remains correct during bounded shutdown: lifecycle code no
  longer clears a live MPSC queue owned by the recorder consumer.
- Normal File driver shutdown is recognized correctly when Java reports
  `ClosedByInterruptException` after clearing the interrupt flag.

These improvements address the cases that matter most in production: a
backend may complete requests late, a client may be saturated, and shutdown
may race with in-flight I/O. A successful SBK 10.7 run now has a stronger
guarantee that its final measurements were actually recorded.

### Highlight: complete S3 and ECS/ObjectScale benchmark controls

The MinIO driver is now a broad S3-compatible benchmark engine, validated
against multi-node Dell ECS/ObjectScale clusters while retaining a minimal
write/read hot path.

- Endpoint pools are validated strictly, credentials cannot be embedded in
  endpoint URLs, and optional all-endpoint preflight identifies a bad node
  before timing starts.
- Endpoint metrics report operation, byte, retry, and failure distribution,
  making round-robin node coverage visible in a clustered run.
- PUT, GET, verified GET, range GET, COPY, STAT, DELETE, tagging, multipart,
  versioning, checksums, request headers, and bucket lifecycle workflows are
  available with explicit validation.
- Range reads support fixed, sequential, and deterministic random aligned
  offsets. LIST workloads support V1/V2, delimiter, start-after/marker,
  owner, metadata, and entry-limit controls.
- Real S3 workload mixes reject duplicate operations and validate finite
  catalog and producer/consumer requirements before a run can stall.
- Mixed reads default to the prepared catalog. The old published-object mode
  is rejected because it can wait indefinitely when writers finish first.
- Retry scheduling provides capped exponential backoff with full jitter, while
  retry totals are surfaced without adding per-success bookkeeping.
- Run manifests are valid JSON and deliberately exclude endpoint URLs,
  credentials, and extra-header values.

The driver also corrects CRC-64/NVME initialization and finalization. Backends
that validate this checksum now accept `-checksum crc64nvme` writes correctly.

### Highlight: accurate metadata and low-rate measurements

Several silent measurement errors are corrected across the framework.

- LIST operations no longer report listed object payload sizes as transferred
  bytes. Metadata benchmarks now report zero object-content bytes rather than
  fabricated bandwidth.
- Byte conversion constants correctly define a GiB, preventing oversized CSV
  rotation limits and incorrect memory-size display.
- Throughput and aggregate-record targets that would truncate below one record
  per worker are rejected instead of silently becoming unlimited saturation.
- Boolean and thread-mode arguments are parsed strictly, so misspellings no
  longer quietly change benchmark behavior.
- CSV numeric output uses a locale-independent decimal separator, preserving
  the header/data column contract in comma-decimal locales.
- Pending request reporting no longer produces negative read/write values, and
  read pending record/byte fields are emitted in their intended order.

### Highlight: exact latency recording with transparent trade-offs

SBK continues to retain exact latency values rather than sampling them. 10.7
adds repeatable JMH evidence rather than making unqualified performance claims.

- The PerL benchmark matrix compares exact array and primitive-map recorders
  with HdrHistogram across sequential and clustered-lognormal workloads and
  from 32 KiB through 32 MiB latency ranges.
- The documentation states the public-API lifecycle difference explicitly:
  PerL extracts configured percentiles and clears occupied array slots in one
  traversal, while normal HdrHistogram use asks for each percentile separately.
- The results identify the real crossover: dense exact arrays are excellent
  for narrow, cache-resident ranges, while HdrHistogram has bounded-footprint
  advantages at broad clustered ranges. The task reports evidence; it does not
  conflate performance with the semantic difference between exact retention
  and quantization.
- PerL and queue microbenchmarks remain available to protect record-path
  latency, allocation, and producer throughput.

### Highlight: safe, driver-scoped containers

SBK containers are opt-in and can be built for one selected driver rather than
shipping every enabled SDK.

- `prepareContainerBuild` produces a deterministic, driver-scoped build
  context and explicit target-to-role/driver mappings.
- Buildx Bake builds SBK, SBM, SBK-YAL, and SBK-GEM-YAL images from that
  context. The standard build, check, release qualification, and publication
  paths remain container-independent.
- JRE bases are used where a compiler is not required; the GEM controller uses
  the JDK base required for remote Java provisioning modules.
- Image entrypoints validate allowed roles and installed launchers, preserve
  a source-archive-friendly revision fallback, and document shutdown behavior
  accurately.

### Highlight: lifecycle resilience from client to SBM and GEM

- SBM drains all queue shards before stopping its consumer and fails bounded
  cleanup rather than silently discarding queued aggregate measurements.
- SBM control-plane callbacks run outside its service monitor, avoiding a slow
  registering client blocking other lifecycle operations.
- PerL executors are closed on orderly completion; recorder shutdown is
  bounded and interruption-aware.
- SBK-GEM preserves remote deployment and benchmark lifecycle diagnostics,
  while normal distributed result output distinguishes complete and failed
  node sets clearly.
- Callback-based readers retain their callback control model; unsupported
  rate-controlled combinations are not silently accepted as valid pacing.

### Engineering quality and contributor safeguards

- `docs/HOT_PATHS.md` is an enforced inventory of per-operation,
  per-measurement, per-window, and lifecycle-critical code paths across PerL,
  SBK, SBM, and SBK-GEM.
- Every supported agent entry point routes contributors to the hot-path policy.
  Changes that add coordination, branching, allocations, or dispatch work to
  the successful record path require explicit developer approval and measured
  evidence.
- Gradle verifies documentation routing, generated artifact packaging, and
  sensitivity-map coverage so guidance cannot silently drift.
- New regression, stress, and release-functional coverage protects queue
  lifecycle ownership, final-result publication, File EOF behavior, shutdown
  interruption handling, generated documentation, and S3 correctness.

## Compatibility notes

- JDK 25 remains the required build and runtime baseline.
- SBP remains at major version 4. Distributed SBK clients and SBM must use
  compatible protocol versions.
- MinIO SDK 8.5.17 remains pinned for compatibility with older ECS,
  ObjectScale, and Ceph S3 implementations. Do not upgrade to MinIO SDK 9.x
  without backend compatibility validation.
- MinIO endpoint configuration is pool-based; obsolete endpoint aliases are
  rejected rather than accepted ambiguously.
- `-mixed-read-source published` is intentionally unavailable because it can
  produce an unbounded reader stall. Use the default `catalog` source.
- A nonzero exit status means benchmark cleanup or a worker failed. Do not use
  a `Total` line from a failed run as an accepted performance result.

## Installation

1. Download `sbk-10.7.tar` or `sbk-10.7.zip` from this release.
2. Verify the archive against `SHA256SUMS`.
3. Extract it, for example: `tar -xvf sbk-10.7.tar`.
4. Run `<extracted-directory>/bin/sbk -help`.

Standalone SBM and SBK Web Console archives are attached. Container users can
pull `kmgowda/sbk:10.7` or `ghcr.io/kmgowda/sbk:10.7` after publication.
